newsitem.title: THAILAND: Thai baht, stocks hit by news of more suspensions.
newsitem.headline: Thai baht, stocks hit by news of more suspensions.

text.p: Thai stocks took a nosedive and the baht sagged on Tuesday following an announcement by the Thai central bank that more than half of the country's finance companies had been suspended, which caught the markets by surprise.
Bank of Thailand governor Chaiyawat Wibulswadi told a news conference that the bank had suspended the operations of 42 finance companies, in addition to 16 already suspended.

The move ignited hectic sales in the stock market as it added to worries over the already troubled financial sector. It also overshadowed a government announcement later in the day on a long-awaited package of measures aimed at pulling the Thai economy out of its worst slump in more than a decade.
The market's benchmark composite SET index ended the session down 2.31 percent to 648.47 after falling more than four percent to hit an intraday low of 634.58.

"Investors rushed and sold those finance firms which were suspended by authorities as soon as the announcement came out. Another announcement which came out later on the approval of measures to boost the economy didn't have much impact," said Chetta Meemangkang of Prime Finance and Securities.
The baht, meanwhile, fell to 31.70/32.00 to the dollar near the close in the domestic market, from 31.20/31.40 in early trade.

"The market had expected only the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) rescue package. The suspension of a large number of finance companies was unexpected and triggered some dollar buying," said one foreign bank trader.
Traders said the suspension news hurt the already-bearish Thai stock market, which had been hit hard by the de facto devaluation of the baht on July 2.

The central bank governor said the suspension will ease the state burden by helping tackle severe liquidity problems, adding that the bank also guaranteed debt repayments and deposits of the troubled companies.
Thai finance companies have been struggling to cope with higher funding costs and deteriorating revenues amid the nation's worst economic crisis in over a decade.
Soon after the central bank announcement, the Thai bourse said it had suspended trading in 17 ailing finance companies.

The news of the suspension dampened earlier optimism that a decision to accept IMF support and to abide by the organisation's tough monetary and fiscal conditions would help extricate Thailand from its financial crisis.
Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya on Tuesday unveiled a series of tough measures to boost the economy, with the goal of winning $12-$15 billion in loans from foreign countries and the IMF.

The Thai government set targets of keeping $25 billion in foreign reserves, cutting the current account deficit, controlling inflation and raising the value-added tax to 10 percent from the current seven percent.
But those steps failed to impress the market, which is still awaiting to see the government backs up its words with action.

"The government must strive to carry out these measures and explain the policy effects in order to send a clear message to assure the financial markets," said Nobuo Nakayama, joint general manager of Sakura Bank Ltd.
